notes.33:18: The Hebrew word shalem is rendered here as "safely" in the sense of wholeness and peace, though some ancient interpreters take it as a proper name, Shalem, a city of Shechem.
notes.33:19: The Hebrew qesitah refers to an ancient unit of weight or currency of uncertain value; in verse 20, the altar name El Elohe Israel means God, the God of Israel.
notes.34:3: The Hebrew idiom translated "spoke tenderly to" literally reads "spoke upon the heart of," signifying comforting and affectionate persuasion.
notes.34:25: The Hebrew adverb betach, rendered "unawares," can indicate either that the city felt secure and unsuspecting or that Simeon and Levi attacked boldly without fear.
notes.34:30: "Making me odious" renders a Hebrew verb meaning literally "to make me a stench," and "few in number" translates literally "men of number."
notes.35:7: The Hebrew pairs the divine title Ha-Elohim ("God") with a plural verb ("revealed Himself"), a construction associated with the plural of majesty.
notes.35:16: The Saints Hebrew Critical Text places the statement that Israel journeyed and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder (Migdal-Eder) at the end of verse 16 rather than as a separate verse 21.
notes.35:18: Ben-Oni means "Son of My Sorrow," while Benjamin means "Son of the Right Hand."
notes.35:22: Masoretic manuscripts mark a mid-verse pause after "and Israel heard of it," underscoring the solemn weight of Reuben's transgression before enumerating Jacob's twelve sons.
notes.36:5: The Hebrew text preserves a consonantal variant (Ketiv: Jeish), while the traditional reading (Qere) is Jeush; the same variant recurs in verse 14.
notes.36:15: The Hebrew term alluph designates a tribal chief or clan leader among the Edomites and Horites.
notes.36:24: The Hebrew word hayyemim occurs only here in Scripture; it is widely understood to mean hot springs, though some older versions rendered it mules.
notes.36:26: The Masoretic Hebrew text reads Dishan here, though this line corresponds to Anah's son Dishon in verse 25 and 1 Chronicles 1:41.
notes.36:39: The Masoretic Hebrew text reads Hadar here, whereas 1 Chronicles 1:50 and several ancient witnesses read Hadad.
notes.37:3: The Hebrew phrase literally suggests an ornate or long-sleeved tunic reaching the palms and ankles; it has traditionally been rendered "tunic of many colors" following the ancient Greek and Latin versions.
notes.37:12: In the Masoretic Text, the direct object marker before "flock" bears extraordinary dots above its letters, an ancient scribal mark traditionally associated with rabbinic reflection on the brothers' intentions.
notes.37:36: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "Medanites" (descendants of Medan, brother of Midian in Genesis 25:2), a kindred group closely associated with the Midianite and Ishmaelite traders in verse 28.
notes.38:14: Enaim (literally "Two Springs" or "Opening of Eyes") refers to a town or landmark situated along the road leading up to Timnah (cf. verse 21).
notes.38:21: Whereas verse 15 uses the ordinary word for a harlot, Hirah and the men of the place use the Hebrew term for a cult or temple harlot connected with Canaanite shrine practices.
notes.38:25: Tamar's appeal "Please identify" repeats the exact Hebrew phrase Judah and his brothers used when presenting Joseph's bloodstained tunic to Jacob in 37:32.
notes.38:29: The name Perez resembles the Hebrew word for "breach" or "breaking through," while Zerah in verse 30 suggests "dawning" or "shining," recalling the scarlet thread.
notes.39:1: Potiphar's title "officer" renders Hebrew saris, denoting a high royal court official; "captain of the guard" is literally "chief of the bodyguards."
notes.39:20: The Masoretic Ketiv reads asurei ("those bound of the king"), while the Qere reads asirei ("the prisoners of the king"), which is followed here. "Prison" renders Hebrew bet hassohar, literally "house of confinement."
notes.39:21: Hebrew chesed ("lovingkindness") denotes the LORD's steadfast covenant mercy and faithful devotion toward Joseph even in confinement.
notes.40:1: Hebrew mashqeh refers to the royal cupbearer, a high-ranking court official entrusted with inspecting and serving the king's drink.
notes.40:16: Hebrew sallei chori is traditionally understood as "baskets of white bread," though some interpreters take chori to denote "openwork" or "wicker" baskets.
notes.40:19: Joseph deliberately echoes the idiom "lift up your head" from verse 13—meaning to reinstate or take account of—with grim irony by adding "from off you" to announce the baker's execution.
notes.41:1: The Hebrew term ye'or is an Egyptian loanword referring specifically to the Nile River.
notes.41:40: The Hebrew verb yishaq is understood either as being ordered or governed by Joseph's command or as paying homage at his word.
notes.41:43: The exclamation abrek is an Egyptian acclamation of homage, traditionally associated in Hebrew with the root meaning to kneel or bow the knee.
notes.41:45: Zaphenath-Paneah is an Egyptian name commonly understood to mean 'God speaks and he lives.'
notes.41:56: Hebrew literally reads 'all that was in them,' referring to all the storehouses in the cities where the grain had been laid up.
notes.42:7: The Hebrew creates a striking wordplay between "recognized them" and "acted as a stranger toward them," both formed from the same verbal root.
notes.42:9: "The nakedness of the land" is a Hebrew idiom denoting the land's exposed, undefended, or vulnerable points.
notes.42:25: Here and throughout chapters forty-two and forty-three, "silver" renders the Hebrew term used for weighed silver serving as money (see 43:21).
notes.42:38: "Sheol" is the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead or the grave.
notes.43:11: "Choice produce" translates a Hebrew phrase literally meaning "the song" or "the prized products of the land."
notes.43:14: "God Almighty" translates the Hebrew divine title El Shaddai.
notes.43:28: The Masoretic Ketiv reads a singular form, whereas the Qere followed here reads the plural ("and prostrated themselves"), agreeing with the preceding plural verb.
notes.43:34: "Five times as great" renders the Hebrew idiom literally meaning "five hands," denoting a fivefold portion.
notes.44:5: The Hebrew emphasizes the verb with an infinitive absolute ('indeed practices divination'), alluding to the ancient Near Eastern custom of seeking omens in liquid poured into a goblet.
notes.44:16: Judah uses a reflexive verb meaning 'justify ourselves' or 'clear ourselves,' confessing that God has uncovered the brothers' deeper past guilt.
notes.44:29: Sheol is the Hebrew term for the grave or realm of the dead; Jacob speaks here of going down 'in affliction' (calamity), and Judah echoes him in 44:31 with 'with grief.'
notes.45:8: The title 'a father to Pharaoh' reflects an ancient Egyptian court designation for a trusted senior counselor and vizier.
notes.45:17: The Hebrew verb translated 'load' appears only here in the Hebrew Bible.
notes.45:24: The Hebrew verb translated 'quarrel' broadly denotes agitation, anger, or trembling, cautioning the brothers against mutual recrimination or turmoil on the journey home.
notes.45:26: The Hebrew idiom 'his heart grew numb' literally describes the heart growing cold or faint in stunned disbelief.
notes.46:15: The total of thirty-three counts Leah's listed sons, grandsons, and Dinah, excluding Er and Onan who died in Canaan, together with Jacob as the head of the line.
notes.46:26: The Hebrew idiom literally reads "those who came forth from his thigh," referring to Jacob's direct physical descendants.
notes.46:27: The Masoretic total of seventy souls combines the sixty-six descendants who traveled down to Egypt with Jacob himself, Joseph, and Joseph's two sons born in Egypt.
notes.47:18: "In the second year" refers to the year following the year in which the Egyptians traded their livestock for bread, not the second year of the seven-year famine.
notes.47:21: The Masoretic Hebrew reads "he removed them into the cities," whereas the Septuagint and Samaritan Pentateuch read "he reduced them to servitude."
notes.47:31: The Masoretic vocalization reads hammittah ("the bed"), whereas the Septuagint, echoed in Hebrews 11:21, vocalizes the same consonants as hammatteh ("the staff").
notes.48:14: The rare Hebrew verb sikkel occurs only here in the Old Testament and denotes either crossing the hands or guiding them with deliberate understanding.
notes.48:16: The Hebrew verb rendered multiply abundantly is derived from the word for fish, conveying the image of teeming, overflowing increase.
notes.48:22: The Hebrew word shekhem means shoulder, mountain ridge, or portion, forming a deliberate wordplay on the city of Shechem.
notes.49:5: The rare Hebrew noun mekherotehem is most widely understood as their swords or knives, though some ancient interpreters took it as their dwellings or compacts.
notes.49:10: Shiloh is traditionally understood as a messianic title; alternatively, the Hebrew form has been interpreted as the one to whom it belongs or as tribute brought to him.
notes.49:19: The Hebrew verse weaves a fourfold soundplay around the name Gad with the words for raiders, shall raid him, and shall raid.
notes.49:26: The Masoretic Hebrew reads horay, meaning my forefathers or progenitors, whereas some ancient versions read a similar consonantal form meaning ancient mountains.
notes.50:5: The Hebrew verb rendered "dug" may denote hewing out a rock-cut tomb or, from a homonymous root, acquiring a burial site by purchase.
notes.50:11: The place name Abel Mizraim plays on the resemblance between the Hebrew words for "mourning" and "meadow," tying the site to the solemn grief of the Egyptians.
notes.50:21: "Spoke to their hearts" renders a Hebrew idiom meaning to speak tenderly, kindly, and reassuringly.
notes.50:23: "Born upon Joseph's knees" is a Hebrew idiom expressing the formal acknowledgment and reception of descendants into the family lineage.
